column4: The owner reports the car when he finds it gone, its plate is known for good and while the deed is hot the patrol stops it on sight, but how long a car theft stays hot and what hours an arrest for it costs are not written.
column5: Every deed kind gets one row in a single table giving how long it stays hot and its arrest hours; a taken car is hot for 3 game days, stopped on sight, and Frank caught in it is arrested for 8 hours and charged.
column6: One deed table: hot days and hours

column4: Fire can be set at any time, is seen and smelt, draws a crowd and the fire brigade, arson is its own deed, and a reported deed brings an officer to the spot and a constable knocking along the street next morning.

A 999 call, even a false one, brings a constable to the spot that night and a rattled bin moves the beat constable off his round, but which officer is drawn, for how long, and whether a false call is noticed are not written.
column5: Police are a counted resource: each call draws the nearest free officer (beat constable first, then the patrol car) for a stated time, leaving his beat uncovered, and a call found false is noted so a second false call from the same box draws a slower answer.
column6: Police as a finite, movable resource

column4: An anonymous call brings a constable that night but never an arrest alone; tracing the call to its box and the witness who saw Frank use it are not written.
column5: Every tip is a claim: the police note the box it came from and ask near it next morning, and anyone who saw Frank at that box holds it as a slot and can tell, so a tip can lead back to the tipster.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Nothing is written about Frank dropping clothing or a finder handing it in.
column5: Anything Frank drops in a chase (cap, scarf, weapon) is a trace in the world: whoever finds it holds the mark slot it carries, and if handed to the police it lets a witness who saw that mark tie it to him, never naming him alone.
column6: Dropped belongings as slot evidence
column8: high: no game tracks dropped hats

column4: A door shut unseen is not searched and Mickey's people never inform on him, but a knock at the office for Frank, and whether the dispatcher lies to the constables, are not written outside the squad's week.
column5: Whoever the police question about Frank, at a door or in a room, answers by one pull-to-talk rule (LH-04's formula used for every case): Mickey's people never inform, lie for him by temper, and officers without cause note the answer and watch the door.
column6: Pull to talk for every questioned person

column4: Garton looks away from a car once for 50 pounds and a second note is refused, a third reported; looking away from a break-in and asking for more next week are not written.
column5: A bought officer's look-away covers one stated deed per payment, and a greedy bought man asks again a game week later at a higher price, as WI-P07 does for witnesses; refusing ends the arrangement and he remembers.
column6: Bought men ask again by greed

column4: Custody is hours, then release without charge or on police bail or a charge; nobody pays bail for him and the firm runs on its floor while he is held.
There is no jump key and no free climbing; set climbing places are ruled in but their places are not written, and roof noise heard by residents is not set.
column5: Set climbing places are written as short routes on the map, each with its height, time and noise reach; if a roof run is one, the sleeping house rule wakes those below and they report a man on the roofs.
column6: Set climbing places as written routes
column11: scope: roof routes in or out

column4: Striking an officer is a deed he remembers by perception and costs 8 hours and a charge, but whether a shove into a hedge counts as a strike is not written.
column5: Every touch on an officer is read by its rung on the escalation ladder: a shove is assault on police, remembered as such, costing 6 hours and a charge if proved, lighter than a blow.
column6: Every touch on an officer read by the ladder

column4: A hidden car is not seen so not stopped, and a paid man remembers being paid, but how the lock-up owner answers police questions is written only for the squad's week.
column5: The pull-to-talk rule covers every person the police ask: the lock-up owner's loyalty, payment and fear set against the deed's weight decide whether he holds, gives a lead or signs.
column6: Pull to talk for every questioned person
column8: high: hidden car as a person

column4: Nothing is written about benefits or the dole office.
column5: Civic matters (dole, council tax, bills) stay off as systems; at most a letter or a line of talk at the soft edge, with a neighbour's tip a talk entry that costs nothing.
column6: Civic paperwork as soft-edge letters
column11: scope: civic paperwork in or out

column4: The poll tax appears only as radio news; summonses and bailiffs are not written.
column5: If civic paperwork is in, each bill is a letter with one deadline and one visit, missed only at a stated cost in money; otherwise it stays as news on the radio.
column6: Civic paperwork as soft-edge letters
column11: scope: poll tax and bailiffs in or out

column4: Nothing is written about bailiffs; the only police visit with notice is Ellis's office search.
column5: If bailiffs are in, a bailiff's return with a constable is a scene with notice like the office search, and what is stored where he looks is found by the same rule.
column6: Civic paperwork as soft-edge letters
column11: scope: poll tax and bailiffs in or out

column4: An alibi stands as long as its giver holds and Mickey's people never inform but lie by temper; an interview alone is written only in the squad's week.
column5: The pull-to-talk rule covers every interview: the driver's loyalty, nerve and fear of Frank against the detective's visits and the deed's weight decide whether he holds, wavers or breaks, with the sign shown first.
column6: Pull to talk for every questioned person
column8: high: no game tests your alibi

column4: An account is kept as claims checked against knowers' slots and the fare book, and a broken account is a piece, but two givers disagreeing is not written.
column5: Every claim to the police carries a time and place; two claims that disagree beyond a stated margin break the account (one piece, as LH-06) and send the detective back to the weaker giver.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Pickpocketing is not a verb; 'frame' is named as a sent verb but nothing defines planting.
column5: Objects can be placed in a pocket, car or room as an act seen like any other; a search finds what is there, and the person found with it is arrested unless he can show where it came from, while anyone who saw Frank place it holds that.
column6: Planted and passed objects as findable things

column4: Seeing a bought officer take money gives Frank a hook he can spend once; photographs and using one to make an officer drop a case are not written.
column5: A recorded fact (photograph, tape, letter) is a hook that stays true even if the holder is gone; spent on an officer, it buys one stated thing (a case dropped, a statement lost) and the officer then acts against Frank by temper.
column6: Hooks from recorded evidence, with counter-moves
column8: high: noir leverage, rare in games

column4: A spent hook is known and remembered by its target, but what he then does is not written.
column5: A target who learns Frank holds a hook on him picks a counter-move by temper: pay, bargain, or move against Frank through what he controls (a statement found, a raid), each with a sign first.
column6: Hooks from recorded evidence, with counter-moves

column4: A hook is spent once; a victim who takes the secret's sting away by telling, then reports the threat, is not written.
column5: A hook works only while its victim keeps the secret: a victim whose temper allows may tell the named person himself, and then sign a statement naming Frank for the threat, which brings an arrest.
column6: Hooks from recorded evidence, with counter-moves

column4: An arrest needs a signed statement from someone who knew it was the man; Frank going in as a witness with a false description is not written.
column5: Frank's statement is a claim like anyone's, checked against what others saw; a false description sends the police after its target only where it fits held facts, and found false it is a lead against Frank.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts
column8: high: lying to police as play

column4: Past his nerve a crewman talks to the police with a sign first; a lighter sentence offered in return is not written.
column5: Under the pull-to-talk rule an offer from the police adds to the pull in proportion to the man's charge and his greed, so a loyal man with a heavy charge can still break.
column6: Pull to talk for every questioned person

column4: A paid solicitor cuts hours and legal visits are never overheard, but sending a warning to an arrested crewman through one is not written.
column5: Under the pull-to-talk rule a warning carried in adds fear and lowers the pull, but a solicitor who will carry it is found only through a go-between, and if it comes out it is a perverting charge.
column6: Pull to talk for every questioned person

column4: Memories never fade and a kept witness who moves to the soft edge can still be found, but reopening a lesser case is not written.
column5: A case stays open while a knower lives: when a witness returns to the Hook, or Ellis reaches investigating, the old deed is asked about again and her held slots count as if new.
column6: Cases stay open while a knower lives

column4: The 'frame' verb is named but not defined, and planting is not written.
column5: Planting by the placed-object rule makes the driver's arrest; the councillor then holds a need Frank can meet, and anyone who saw the plant holds it against Frank.
column6: Planted and passed objects as findable things

column4: Playing rivals off with lies is written; playing two officers off is not.
column5: Officers are people with temper and memory who share what they hold only through station talk; a different story told to each is believed if it fits what that officer holds, and found out when they compare, at a stated chance per week.
column6: Officers as people with temper and memory

column4: A colleague who sees an officer bought keeps it, and in the squad's week the payments can come out, but what an honest officer does on finding it is not written.
column5: An officer who learns a colleague is bought acts by her temper: high law reports him (a corruption charge and Frank named as payer), low law asks Frank for her share, each shown first.
column6: Officers as people with temper and memory

column4: Giving Ellis a rival removes one charge; a month of being ignored is not written.
column5: A trade with the police buys one stated thing, a charge removed or Ellis's stage held for two game weeks, never a licence, and the rival's people may learn who gave him up.
column6: Police bargains with stated terms

column4: A car on a rank can give an alibi and claims are checked against the fare book and knowers, but only in the squad's week.
column5: Every claim to the police is checked against held facts and records in any case: a fare picked up across town, logged and remembered by the passenger, stands as an alibi while the crew's job is traced only through what its witnesses saw.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Claims are checked against the fare book and knowers' slots in the squad's week; a forged entry checked against its passenger is not written.
column5: A fare-book entry is a claim: a detective checking it asks the named passenger, who holds no slot of the ride unless real, so a forged entry with no real fare breaks the account.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: While Frank is held the firm runs on its floor with Pauline dispatching; a rival using the hold is not written.
column5: Rivals read Frank's absence as an opening: a hold over a stated length lets the nearest rival press a rank or a driver once, shown to Frank on his return.
column6: Rivals read Frank's absence as an opening

column4: Constables knock along the street next morning and anyone can be talked to, but whether a resident tells Frank what she told the police is not written.
column5: Who told whom is a held fact: a resident who spoke to the police remembers it and tells Frank by her temper and regard, and Frank asking after the police is itself seen and told.
column6: Who told whom is itself a held fact

column4: A whereabouts claim is checked against the fare book and the knowers in the squad's week; for an ordinary inquiry it is not.
column5: Every alibi claim is checked against the fare book and the named fare in any case, with the fare's own memory deciding whether it holds.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: In the squad's week each visit adds to her pull and an alibi lasts as long as its giver holds; ordinary second visits are not written.
column5: The pull-to-talk rule runs on every visit in any case, so a nervous alibi giver can change her story on the second visit, with her look away as the sign first.
column6: Pull to talk for every questioned person

column4: Prints on smooth surfaces are compared by hand in days and name Frank only if his prints are on file from an earlier arrest.
Gloves leave no prints but are a mark at night and carry blood.
Blood group is evidence but there is no DNA database; how it counts against a suspect outside the long heat is not written.
column5: 1990 forensics compare and never name: blood group, fibres and prints add a lower piece only against a man already suspected, using the LH-06 count for every serious reported deed.
column6: 1990 forensics compare, never name

column4: Blood comes off with water and privacy; an impounded car and traces left in it are not written.
column5: Traces in a car follow the compare rule: washing removes what shows, but a car seized in a serious case keeps one hidden trace a search finds unless the seats are replaced, adding a lower piece against a suspect.
column6: 1990 forensics compare, never name

column4: Nothing is written about a police pound or forged papers.
column5: Seized property follows one return rule: a seized car is held a game week as WI-P03's envelope, returned only to its keeper in person, and forgery is not a verb.
column6: Seized property follows one return rule

column4: Charges accumulate and are read at the ending; a dropped lesser charge and an officer's grudge are not written.
column5: Officers are people with temper and memory: a dropped charge leaves the list, and an arresting officer with high temper gives Frank cause at every challenge for two game weeks, shown in how he speaks.
column6: Officers as people with temper and memory

column4: Lesser charges end in police bail and only a killing charge has magistrates and remand; bail for a crewman and skipping it are not written.
column5: Anyone charged follows one bail rule: police bail for lesser charges, remand for a killing, and a man who skips bail is wanted on sight and adds a charge, his crewmates questioned.
column6: Bail and remand for anyone charged

column4: Ron's remand uses LH-07's scenes and a social visit is overheard when the visitor's nerve is low; Frank visiting a crewman is not written.
column5: The remand rule runs both ways: Frank visiting a held man is a social visit he can use to learn what was said, overheard when either man's nerve is below the middle.
column6: Bail and remand for anyone charged

column4: Two named officers can be bought; regard with an honest constable is not written.
column5: Officers have regard like anyone: friendship lets an honest constable talk Frank round on suspicion alone, never on a deed he sees, and the station never changes.
column6: Officers as people with temper and memory

column4: The constable challenges on suspicion where a man should not be and remembers like anyone; his pocketbook holds the day's names, but loitering on repeat nights is not written.
column5: An officer notes each sighting in his pocketbook and a pattern (the same man at the same place three nights) gives him cause at the next challenge and talk to Ellis.
column6: Officer pocketbook and pattern noticing

column4: A constable challenges on suspicion, a man who stands is searched for what is under his coat and a weapon found means arrest.
Nothing is written about passing a weapon to someone before a search.
column5: A passed object is a placed object: the passer-by holds it and the sight of Frank handing it over, and reports by the 2.5.2 formula with a weapon as the deed's weight.
column6: Planted and passed objects as findable things

column4: An anonymous call brings a constable but no arrest; walking into the station to report is written only for handing himself in.
column5: Every report is a claim checked against held facts: Frank's report at the counter names him as its source, brings a search of the lock-up next day, and what is found there counts against its holder.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Only phone tips are written; letters are not.
column5: An anonymous letter is a tip like a call: it brings a look at the place within two game days, never an arrest alone, and what is found counts.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Ellis's office search always comes with notice the evening before, and a bought Ellis once tells Frank which knower is seen next.
In the squad's week a bought man's nerve decides whether he names Frank when the station is leaned on; an outside corruption inquiry is not written otherwise.
column5: Officers are people with temper and memory: any inquiry that leans on a bought man runs his nerve, and past it he names Frank as payer, adding a corruption charge.
column6: Officers as people with temper and memory

column4: Seeing a bribe gives a hook; a secret tape is not written.
column5: A tape is a recorded hook, as a photograph: it stays true if Frank is gone and buys one stated thing once, after which the officer counters by temper.
column6: Hooks from recorded evidence, with counter-moves

column4: Planting is not written, and a call-box tip never makes an arrest alone.
column5: By the placed-object rule goods put in a rival's car are found by the search a tip brings, and the rival is arrested unless he can show where they came from.
column6: Planted and passed objects as findable things

column4: Nothing is written about tracing repeated calls.
column5: Each tip notes its box, and the same box used again draws a constable to watch it at that hour; anyone who sees Frank there holds that slot.
column6: Officer pocketbook and pattern noticing

column4: Fencing is written and an office-search find is a handling charge, but a thief who names Frank when arrested is not written.
column5: The pull-to-talk rule applies to every arrested person: a thief who knows Frank bought from him gives a lead, and the police call at the office.
column6: Pull to talk for every questioned person

column4: Nothing lets another person confess to Frank's deed.
column5: A confession is a claim checked against the scene: believed only if it fits the held slots and pieces, and a mismatch turns the police toward who he shields.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: A witness can take her statement back, and a poor-conditions sighting counts 1 not 3; eyesight is not a stored fact.
column5: Her sight conditions are held facts; persuading her to claim worse ones is a take-back by WI-P07, checked against what others saw of her that night.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: The office can be watched in the squad's week, but an observation post is not written.
column5: Every police watch has a world sign: an observation post shows as a lit window and a man who comes and goes at shift change, readable if Frank looks.
column6: Every police watch has a world sign

column4: The car is a mark slot and a cab with its roof sign is named as the firm's; how the police then find which driver is not written.
column5: A firm car seen is a lead to the firm: the police ask who drove it, the board and fare book answer, and Pauline's answer follows the pull-to-talk rule.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: What Frank says when he hands himself in counts as an admission; words said at arrest otherwise are not written.
column5: Frank's words to an officer are claims stored as said; an admission counts as LH-06's piece in any case, and a taunt with no fact in it counts as nothing.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Frank can talk a witness round, and her regard, ties and temper decide whether she yields or takes a statement back.
Giving Ellis a rival removes one of Frank's charges, but the police lying in wait at a rival's job is not written.
column5: A trade with the police buys one stated thing: a tip that fits held facts brings officers to the stated place and time, and if the rival's crew come they are arrested, while his people may learn who gave him up.
column6: Police bargains with stated terms

column4: Paying a rival's man to inform is written; police informants are not.
column5: Informants are named people with a price: a detective's informant has temper and loyalty like a rival's man, can be bought by the WI-P06 rule, and is found out at a stated chance.
column6: Informants as named people with a price

column4: A second note to Garton after his one look-away is refused and a third reported; an honest constable takes a bribe as a crime he saw.
Anyone down can be searched and a found book can give hooks, but names handed to a detective are not written.
column5: Names given to the police are claims checked against held facts: each named man holding a matching slot is asked, and the detective asks Frank how he came by them.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: The station is a soft-edge scene reached only to hand himself in; a lie is checked against what the officer holds.
column5: The front counter is a short scene for any visit (reporting, handing in, asking), where a false name is checked against what the desk holds and a car left running outside is a give-away.
column6: The station front counter as a scene

column4: A call from one of three boxes brings a constable; a call as an alibi is not written.
column5: A call is a claim with a place and time: it puts the caller at that box, which helps only if someone saw him there and harms if it does not fit what witnesses hold.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: The station as a whole never changes; gossip about an officer reaching his sergeant is not written.
column5: Talk about an officer reaches the station only as talk and never sacks him; the officer learns where it came from and grows cooler to Frank.
column6: Officers as people with temper and memory

column4: Nothing lets anyone confess in Frank's place.
column5: A confession is checked against what witnesses hold: a stranger's account that fails their slots is not believed and turns the police to who paid him.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Nothing is written about handing in property or earning police goodwill.
column5: An officer's regard moves with what Frank does for him: a kindness raises it a little, buying an easier talk-round on suspicion only, never a deed overlooked.
column6: Officers as people with temper and memory

column4: There are no fines as a system and nothing wipes a memory or a record.
The station is a soft-edge scene; standing in its front office is not written.
column5: The front counter is a short scene: Frank can say his piece and leave, and staying past it the desk sergeant asks him to go, then cautions him.
column6: The station front counter as a scene

column4: Custody is a short scene of under 2 real minutes in which the hours pass and he is released; there is nothing to refuse.
Nothing is written about handing objects to the police as evidence.
column5: Anything handed in is a claim checked against held facts: blank pages are no lead and the officer remembers a time-waster; a stolen police pocketbook handed back is a deed found.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Nothing is written about Frank giving a statement as a witness.
column5: Frank's statement is a claim: putting himself at the scene is a lower piece against him, and a version that fits his own deed reads as an admission.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: Talk alone brings questions, never an arrest; whether people who hear Frank's own boasts carry them is not written.
column5: Frank's own words are held facts for whoever hears them: a boast is told on as talk, brings Ellis's asking round, and never an arrest without a signed statement.
column6: Frank's own words as held facts

column4: An anonymous call brings a constable that night; describing a bystander is not written.
column5: A tip is a claim: the constable comes and checks the described man against what is held, finds nothing, and the man beside Frank heard every word and remembers it.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts

column4: An account is classified into claims by the model and checked by the Core; nonsense speech is not written.
column5: Speech with no claim in it gives no claim: the detective names the evasion, records nothing, and the interview ends as no account.
column6: Claims to police checked against held facts
